newsitem.title: USA: Molycorp sees Questa mine on track in Feb.
newsitem.headline: Molycorp sees Questa mine on track in Feb.

text.p: Molycorp, the Unocal Corp subsidiary, said its troubled Questa molybdenum mine in New Mexico will be on track in February, four months after start-up last October, company officials said.
"We are producing material and we are going through some typical start-up problems," Greg Cynor, Molycorp's marketing manager said.
"I think we are getting them under control and they are behind us. We will be where we should be in February," Cynor added.
When Molycorp's intention to reopen Questa - an asset which Unocal has tried to offload in the past - first became known last year, the intimate world of moly shivered.
Fears that the extra material could not be absorbed easily - coupled with some heavy Chinese selling at the time - caused moly prices stumble, traders said.
In Japan, traders said on Tuesday that offers for moly oxide had risen to $4.70 per pound Mo amid strong domestic demand and talk of supply difficulties in North America such as delays at Molycorp.
Molycorp, however, was tight lipped about detailing the start-up problems, or saying how much concentrates it was shipping or the level of production expected this year.
Cynor also declined to say whether Molycorp was selling its concentrates or converting some of the output.
Traders said Molycorp's situation was "confused" and the company's intentions unclear.
There was talk that Molycorp was or intended to convert the concs into oxide or ferro-moly at a roasting plant in Washington, Pennsylvania.
In the U.S. moly oxide was quoted at $4.40 to $4.60 per pound Mo delivered to consumer's works.
Another North American producer said although there were initial fears about Molycorp's output disrupting the market, those concerns have eased.
"I would say right now it's not that big a deal - the market looks like it can absorb it pretty well," the producer official said.
But Tom Hobbs, moly marketing manager at Kennecott Utah Copper, part of RTZ Corp, said the market was depending on Questa's output, put at 10 to 12 million pounds a year, to maintain equilibrium.
Kennecott forecast that Western world supply and demand were roughly 225 million pounds in 1996, with demand expected to grow 3 to 5 percent in 1997.
"The increase in consumption should be met by Questa," Hobbs said.

Kennecott produced about 24 million pounds of molybdenum in 1996 at its Bingham Canyon mine in Utah, some 4 million pounds higher than originally planned because of better ore grades. Moly is a byproduct from Kennecott's copper output.
"The plan this year is to produce 20 million pounds," Hobbs added.
Meanwhile Thompson Creek's mine in Idaho is still producing at capacity despite the harsh weather in the North West, sources close to the company said.
But some in the moly industry are still surprised that Questa, a small, primary mine whose production costs are not among the lowest in the industry, was reopened in the first place.
"Maybe its easier to sell it as a going concern than as something that's mothballed," an industry source said.
((Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1640))
